GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The next chance for impactful weather comes next week as a low pressure system traverses the West. Ahead of this system, southwesterly flow will begin to direct moisture towards the region as early as Monday.
GJT.text:
With high pressure driving the forecast, sunny days, clear nights, and dry conditons continue through the weekend. A Freeze Warning remains in effect tonight for parts of northwest Colorado and CO Zone 23 in southwest Colorado with another night of sub-freezing temperatures expected. Most locations within the Freeze Warning also saw a hard freeze last night.

Otherwise, seasonable to seasonably cool daytime temperatures highlight the forecast through the weekend.

The next chance for impactful weather comes next week as a low pressure system traverses the West. Ahead of this system, southwesterly flow will begin to direct moisture towards the region as early as Monday. As a result, isolated convection is possible over the southern Mountains early in the week. By mid- week, an uptick in synoptic forcing could increase the coverage of showers and storms across the region. It's too early to pin down the potential hazards associated with this system, but expect increasingly unsettled weather as the week progresses.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: We are watching the arrival of this next storm system for the latter portions of next week, when the West Coast trough pushes east across the Rockies.
BOU.text:
A rather chilly day is unfolding despite full sunshine. Clear skies, light winds, and a dry airmass will allow strong radiational cooling tonight, with below freezing temperatures expected over most of the northeast plains again. Meanwhile, we'll see a light downslope component develop along the Front Range keeping most of Denver/Boulder areas a few degrees warmer. Most locations northeast of Denver observed a hard killing freeze last night (deemed as 28F or colder), so from this point forward we will only be issuing highlights for those areas where a killing freeze did not occur - namely the I-25 Corridor and far northeast corner of the state. That means a Freeze Warning for Sedgwick and Phillips Counties tonight where lows are expected to dip into the mid to upper 20s.

For Saturday, an upper level ridge will build overhead with sunny skies and dry weather. Temperatures will be warming with highs pushing into the upper 60s to mid 70s, a few degrees above normal. Overall, another day of light winds can be expected with high pressure in control. There will just a slight increase of southerly winds over the eastern plains, resulting in localized elevated fire weather conditions mainly over Lincoln and Washington Counties.

On Sunday, the upper level ridge axis will shift eastward with light southwest flow aloft developing. This supports a continuation of above normal temperatures, with highs pushing into the 70s again across most of the plains. Enough mid level moisture gets caught up in this flow to warrant a low chance of showers in the mountains by Monday and Tuesday. That chance of showers may very well increase Wednesday, depending on how much tropical moisture pulls northward in advance of the next trough digging southward off the West Coast.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Although the ContDvd is likely to see quite a bit of precip, temps are unseasonably warm, so snow levels will likely be quite high, The best chance for substantial accumulating snow over most of the mtns will not occur until the trough is actually moving over the region, and this will not occur until mid to late week.
PUB.text:
The good new in the long term forecast is we are likely to see quite a bit of precipitation during this period over the western sections of the forecast area, especially along the San Juan mountains. By Sunday, moisture will increase over the southwest US and push to the northeast. Showers will develop over the San Juans by late Sunday as a weak disturbance over the SW moves over the region. A more substantial trough is forecast to develop over the Pacific Northwest Monday and then slowly amplify and drop south-southeast through the week. This trough promises to bring much more substantial moisture to the San Juans by mid week. This troughiness is expected to continue over the region into next weekend.

For the remainder of the region, especially the plains, It will likely remain dry and unseasonably warm. Expect max temps on the plains to be in the 70s to around 80F during this period, which is about 15 degrees above normal for this time of the year. The best chance of some precip over the lower elevations will not occur until next weekend.

Although the ContDvd is likely to see quite a bit of precip, temps are unseasonably warm, so snow levels will likely be quite high, The best chance for substantial accumulating snow over most of the mtns will not occur until the trough is actually moving over the region, and this will not occur until mid to late week. \/Hodanish

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Mostly benign conditions to start the work week in the long term, but this pattern should begin to be broken up by a deep Pacific system that will encroach our region by the end of the forecast period.
CYS.text: Mostly benign conditions to start the work week in the long term, but this pattern should begin to be broken up by a deep Pacific system that will encroach our region by the end of the forecast period. Monday starts with high pressure ridging mostly holding control of our forecast area, but a weakening upper level low will move across the Four Corners region and then just to our southeast through Tuesday afternoon. While mostly non- impactful, this feature will at least bring a very low end chance of some high elevation precipitation, along with a small bump in moisture. This influx of moisture will continue through the rest of the week as our upper level flow turns southwesterly while we sit between high pressure controlling the southeastern US and a deep Pacific system that will move inland by later Wednesday into Thursday. This feature will be the next noteworthy system to impact the forecast area as we see precipitation begin overspreading late Thursday into Friday and start another cooling trend that should persist into the weekend. For this forecast period, expect mostly similar temperatures day to day as highs will be around 6 to 12 degrees above normal, generally in the 60's to 70's, with lows similarly warm in the 40's. Any drop in temperatures would occur just beyond the long term after the Pacific system moves in, and the most impactful precipitation chances similarly just beyond this forecast time as well. Overall it should be a quiet period, but that will be ending by the weekend after next.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: With the cutoff nature of the low, there is not much of a cold air tap, with 700 mb temps only falling to around 0C to -3C later Thursday into the weekend as the trough axis works in.
SLC.text:
Morning water vapor analysis shows ridging extending through the Great Basin while a broad cutoff low swirls near the Baja Peninsula. With dry and stable conditions, overnight lows dipped near to slightly below freezing in some locations, but temperatures are quickly rebounding. Forecast afternoon highs are expected to push to near seasonable levels in most locations, with the exception being portions of the San Rafael Swell and Castle Country where highs will run around 5-10 degrees below normal.

The broad cutoff low will gradually shift east to northeastward into the Desert Southwest, before ejecting into the northern stream Sunday into Monday. For Saturday, conditions more or less look like a repeat of Friday but with temperatures nudging upwards slightly. Moisture associated with the low will start to push through portions of southern Utah Sunday morning into the afternoon, bringing enhanced cloud cover as well as isolated chances for showers and perhaps a thunderstorm or two. After an overnight lull, similar conditions are then expected Monday.

A larger northern stream trough will be digging southward from the PacNW on Tuesday. Models generally support this feature gradually cutting off from California into the Great Basin through the middle of the week, eventually translating eastward through the Intermountain West on into the weekend. Ensembles mean PWAT anomalies generally push into the 150-200% of normal range (AI ECM locally up to 250% across the Four Corners region). That said, there are some differences in exact timing, likely owing to the cutoff nature of the trough. Overall though, the general pattern would contain enhanced upper and midlevel support, which in combination with ample moisture would result in more widespread precipitation chances across the area. BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Through the week, a high amplitude trough will become a cut off low in southern California and linger in the Great Basin. As the trough builds along the West Coast Monday evening, increasing clouds and breezy conditions in SE Oregon are expected.
BOI.text: Through the week, a high amplitude trough will become a cut off low in southern California and linger in the Great Basin. As the trough builds along the West Coast Monday evening, increasing clouds and breezy conditions in SE Oregon are expected. Residual dry conditions with the wind will support elevated fire weather, though impacts will be minimal as the low continues to move in. Temperatures will cool off Tuesday as a front moves through, cooling temperatures down to near-normal; low-mid 60s for the afternoon high in lower elevations, low 50s for mountain valleys. Ensemble guidance largely favors another cold front on Thursday as the low moves weakens and rejoins the broader flow. This will lead to even cold temperatures, about 5 degrees below normal, Thursday and Friday. Colder temps are accompanied by the best chances for precipitation across much of the area, with valley rain and mountain snow possible.
